I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

vignette: Leila had always been a meticulous person, but since the motor vehicle collision that nearly took her life six months ago, she found herself becoming increasingly withdrawn. It started with small things - hearing the name "Emily" (her best friend's name) would suddenly transport her back to the moment of impact, and she'd find herself questioning whether she should have swerved left instead of right. The uncertainty about what could have been done differently gnawed at her. As time went by, these triggers only intensified. Arguments with her husband, Tuan, over seemingly mundane things would escalate into full-blown fights, leaving Leila feeling lost and anxious. She'd try to reason with herself that it was just a normal disagreement, but the uncertainty about whether she could have prevented the accident seeped into every aspect of their relationship. "What if I'm not good enough?" she'd wonder. To cope with these overwhelming emotions, Leila started avoiding physical stress - anything that put her body under tension made her feel like she was back in the wreckage, fighting for air. She stopped attending yoga classes and took the elevator instead of stairs at work, even though it meant getting to meetings late. Her job as a Database Administrator allowed her to work from home some days, which became more frequent as she found it increasingly difficult to face the crowded office spaces. Avoiding friends was another strategy Leila employed - seeing them only made her feel like an outsider, watching their carefree lives through a distorted lens of guilt and self-blame. She'd convinced herself that if only she'd driven slower, or taken a different route, none of this would have happened. Her mind kept replaying the accident, each iteration leading to more what-ifs and could-haves. In darker moments, Leila resorted to self-harm as a distraction from the relentless thoughts. A few scratches on her wrist or a burned hand seemed like small prices to pay for temporary reprieve from the constant barrage of "if onlys". Her husband found out once, and his worry only added to her feelings of guilt - she was convinced that if she wasn't so broken, he wouldn't be stuck with this anxious, damaged version of Leila. The mistrust had seeped into every corner of her life. Tuan tried to reassure her, but even his words felt like empty promises - after all, people couldn't be trusted to keep their word, just as she hadn't been able to trust herself that day on the road. This constant self-doubt led Leila down a vicious cycle: the more she avoided physical stress and social interactions, the more isolated she became; the more isolated she was, the more her negative appraisals took hold. One evening, as Leila sat at home alone (Tuan had gone out to meet friends, trying to coax her into joining), she realized that this existence couldn't go on. She thought of all the times she'd hurt herself and felt only temporary relief; the arguments with Tuan that left them both drained; and the lost friendships - she couldn't keep living in this half-existence. The weight of it finally brought Leila to seek help, her greatest fear being that she might never break free from this self-reinforcing cycle, forever trapped in a world of what-ifs and could-haves. Leila sat on the couch, surrounded by the familiar walls of her home, yet felt like an outsider looking in. As she waited for her appointment with the therapist, she couldn't help but wonder - would anyone be able to show her that this wasn't all there was?
